[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Tutorial: Docker Logging Drivers and Centralized Logging"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Docker captures standard output (stdout) and standard error (stderr) from your containers and stores them as JSON files on the host machine. In production environments, managing these logs locally becomes inefficient. This tutorial covers how to configure different logging drivers and route container logs to a centralized logging system."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A running Docker environment."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Basic familiarity with Docker containers and Docker Compose."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 1: Understanding Default Local Logging"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Every time you spin up a container without specifying a logging driver, Docker uses the json-file driver. You can inspect a container's current logging driver by executing the following command:"},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"docker inspect -f "{{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Type}}" <container_name>"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 2: Configuring Log Rotation"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Uncapped json-file logs can quickly consume all disk space on your host. You should configure log rotation globally in the Docker daemon configuration file located at /etc/docker/daemon.json."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  }
}"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"After updating the daemon.json file, restart the Docker service to apply the changes:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"sudo systemctl restart docker"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 3: Using Alternative Logging Drivers"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Docker supports many logging drivers like syslog, journald, fluentd, and awslogs. You can specify a driver at runtime using the --log-driver flag."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"docker run -d --name my_app --log-driver syslog --log-opt syslog-address="udp://1.2.3.4:514" nginx"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 4: Centralized Logging with Docker Compose"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"For multi-container applications, centralized logging drivers are best configured via Docker Compose. Below is an example using the fluentd driver to forward logs to an external aggregator."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"version: "3.8"
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    logging:
      driver: "fluentd"
      options:
        fluentd-address: "localhost:24224"
        tag: "docker.web""},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"You have successfully learned how to inspect Docker logging drivers, enforce local log rotation to prevent disk exhaustion, and route logs to external aggregation pipelines using drivers like syslog and fluentd."}]
